events.title: Janet Jackson Super Bowl Halftime
events.blurb: An American pop singer, performing with Justin Timberlake at a Super Bowl halftime show, experienced a "wardrobe malfunction" — Timberlake pulled at her leather bustier at the end of their duet, exposing her right breast for 9/16ths of a second on live television. The incident produced an estimated $550,000 in regulatory fines, congressional hearings, and a lawsuit that reached the Supreme Court. It effectively launched YouTube (co-founder Jawed Karim said later that the desire to re-watch the moment inspired the site). Timberlake's career was barely touched; Jackson's was permanently diminished.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 2004 — Super Bowl XXXVIII halftime show in Houston. The word "wardrobe malfunction" entered the English language. A 2020 retrospective documentary drew new attention to how asymmetrically the American public had blamed Jackson.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: William and Kate Wedding
events.blurb: The 28-year-old second-in-line heir to the British throne married his 29-year-old university sweetheart at Westminster Abbey in London before a congregation of 1,900 and a global TV audience estimated at 2 billion. The bride wore a long-sleeved ivory lace gown; the couple kissed twice on the Buckingham Palace balcony. The marriage, closely followed by the British tabloids for years, has so far produced three children and remained notably less turbulent than the equivalent royal marriage of the generation before.
events.revealBlurb: April 29, 2011 — Prince William and Catherine Middleton. William succeeded his father Charles as Prince of Wales when Charles became king in September 2022. Their three children, in line to the throne: George (2013), Charlotte (2015), Louis (2018).

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Ice Bucket Challenge
events.blurb: A viral social-media fundraising campaign for ALS — amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, commonly called Lou Gehrig's disease — swept the internet over the summer. Participants filmed themselves dumping a bucket of ice water on their heads, challenged friends to do the same, and donated to an ALS charity. Celebrities from Bill Gates to Donald Trump to LeBron James participated. The campaign raised $115 million for ALS research over two months and funded the discovery of a significant ALS-related gene.
events.revealBlurb: Peak: August 2014. The campaign was co-founded by Pete Frates, an ALS patient who died of the disease in 2019. The ALS Association estimated $230 million in total donations. Subsequent research identified the NEK1 gene as a contributor to ALS, directly attributable to the challenge funds.

events.title: Machiavelli Writes The Prince
events.blurb: An unemployed former Florentine civil servant, exiled from the city after a change of regime, wrote a compact political treatise in the form of advice to a hereditary ruler on how to acquire and maintain power. Its flat, unsentimental analysis of the uses of cruelty, deception, and popular love versus fear shocked readers and made its author's name a by-word for cynical politics. It remained unpublished until five years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: 1513 — Niccolò Machiavelli. The treatise was dedicated to Lorenzo de' Medici, who almost certainly never read it. Published 1532 and promptly placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. Still in print 500 years later.

events.title: Johnson's Dictionary Published
events.blurb: An Oxford-educated English essayist, working nine years with six assistants in a garret flat, completed and published a two-volume dictionary of the English language — the first comprehensive, systematically illustrated dictionary of the vernacular. It defined 42,773 words with 114,000 quotations showing their use. It was the standard English dictionary until Oxford's larger project finally superseded it 173 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1755 — Samuel Johnson. He defined "lexicographer" as "a harmless drudge, that busies himself in tracing the original, and detailing the signification of words." His tart definitions became famous in their own right: "Oats: A grain, which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people."

events.title: Pride and Prejudice Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old unmarried English rector's daughter living quietly with her widowed mother in Hampshire published, anonymously, her second novel — a comedy of manners about five daughters of a small landowner, an arrogant wealthy suitor, and a perceptive heroine who misreads them both. The first edition of 1,500 copies was a modest success; the author made £140 from it. She would die four years later; her anonymity was preserved until a posthumous edition named her.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1813 — Jane Austen, attributed to "By the Author of Sense and Sensibility." She sold the copyright outright for £110; her estate never profited further. Austen is now the most continuously read English novelist. A first edition sold at auction in 2008 for £105,000.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: First Iron Bridge Opens
events.blurb: A cast-iron arch bridge opened across a gorge of the Severn River in western England, the first substantial bridge anywhere in the world constructed entirely of iron. Its five parallel ribs, each cast as a single 21-metre piece, spanned 30 metres and weighed 384 tonnes. The bridge was built partly as a structural demonstration by a local ironmaster promoting the capabilities of his foundries.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1781 — Ironbridge, Shropshire. Designer Thomas Farnolls Pritchard, ironmaster Abraham Darby III. It still stands as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The surrounding gorge is considered the cradle of the Industrial Revolution.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: Fall of Monte Cassino
events.blurb: After four separate offensives spanning five months, Polish troops raised their flag over the ruins of a hilltop monastery that had been reduced to rubble by an Allied bombing raid — finally cracking a mountain defensive line that had blocked the Allied advance up a peninsula for half a year and cost over 43,000 casualties across all the assaulting armies.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1944. Polish Corps commander General Anders had promised his men they would fight for Poland in the west since the Soviet Union had taken the east. Over 900 Polish soldiers died in the final assault. The monastery's Benedictine monks had evacuated its art treasures months earlier; the abbey itself was empty during the famous Allied bombing of February 15.

events.title: Yalta Conference
events.blurb: Three heads of government convened at a palatial Crimean resort to decide the political geography of the postwar world — agreeing on the division of a defeated nation into occupation zones, the formation of a new international peace organisation, and the borders of several countries whose populations had no vote in the matter.
events.revealBlurb: February 4–11, 1945. FDR was visibly ill — he would be dead in two months — and Soviet diplomats exploited his eagerness for a deal. Stalin's concessions on free elections in Eastern Europe proved worthless within two years. Churchill reportedly told his doctor: "I do not suppose that at any moment in history has the agony of the world been so great or widespread."

events.title: Victory in Europe Day
events.blurb: Unconditional surrender documents were signed at an Allied headquarters on two successive nights in two different cities, and the moment the ceasefire took effect at one minute past eleven, millions of people in cities across a battered continent poured into the streets to celebrate the end of a conflict that had killed an estimated 70 to 85 million human beings.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1945. Germany signed the first surrender at Reims on May 7; a second signing in Berlin satisfied Soviet demands. Stalin proclaimed May 9 as Victory Day — still observed in Russia today. More than a million people celebrated in the streets across the UK. Churchill told the crowds from a Whitehall balcony: "God bless you all. This is your victory."

events.title: Boston Massacre
events.blurb: A confrontation between a hostile crowd of several hundred colonists and a squad of nine British soldiers on a snow-covered Boston street ended with the soldiers firing into the mob, killing five men. The deaths — including Crispus Attucks, a formerly enslaved sailor of African and Indigenous descent — were immediately weaponized as propaganda, with Paul Revere producing an engraving that circulated throughout the colonies.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1770 — King Street, Boston. John Adams, who would become America's second president, defended the British soldiers in court and won acquittals for six of the eight — calling it one of the best things he ever did for his country. Attucks is often called the first American to die for independence.

events.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events.blurb: American militia who had occupied two hills on a peninsula north of Boston overnight were assaulted by British regulars advancing uphill in three waves. The defenders — reportedly told "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" to conserve ammunition — inflicted heavy casualties on the first two waves before running out of powder and being driven from the ground. The British held the field but lost over 1,000 men; the American cause gained enormous moral prestige.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1775 — fought mostly on Breed's Hill; misnamed after the adjacent Bunker Hill. British commander: General Thomas Gage. American commander killed in the retreat: General Joseph Warren. Within days, Congress appointed George Washington commander-in-chief.

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Franco-American Alliance
events.blurb: A French-American treaty signed in Paris transformed the American rebellion into a global war. France, which had been secretly funneling weapons and volunteers to the rebels through front companies, formally recognized American independence, committed its navy to the war, and in return secured commercial terms with the new republic. Spain joined the next year, the Netherlands the year after, and Britain soon found herself fighting Europe's great powers on multiple oceans.
events.revealBlurb: February 6, 1778 — Treaty of Alliance, Paris. Benjamin Franklin, the Americans' chief diplomat, had worked the French court for two years in a coonskin cap that French aristocrats found exotically charming. France's participation in the war contributed significantly to its own fiscal collapse a decade later.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: Jaws Released
events.blurb: A 28-year-old director released a 124-minute thriller about a great white shark terrorizing a New England beach resort. Principal photography, supposed to last 55 days, ran 159; the mechanical shark broke down constantly and was rarely shown, producing the film's signature off-screen menace. Released across a record number of screens nationwide with a saturation TV ad campaign, it invented the summer blockbuster.
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1975 — Steven Spielberg. The shark's malfunctions forced Spielberg to rely on John Williams' two-note score to telegraph the threat. The film caused a measurable drop in US beach attendance for years afterward.

events.title: Parasite Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A 50-year-old South Korean director's satirical thriller about a poor family insinuating itself into a wealthy family's household became the first non-English-language film to win the top prize at a major U.S. film awards ceremony. It also took Best Director, Best Original Screenplay, and Best International Feature — a quadruple sweep by a "foreign" film that industry observers had long thought impossible. The director thanked Martin Scorsese in one of his acceptance speeches.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 2020 — Bong Joon-ho's "Parasite" at the 92nd Academy Awards. The film's Korean-language narrative beat Sam Mendes's "1917" and Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood." It was also the first Palme d'Or winner to win Best Picture in 65 years.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Harvey Publishes De Motu Cordis
events.blurb: A 50-year-old English royal physician published a 72-page Latin treatise correctly describing, for the first time, the circulation of the blood — with the heart as a muscular pump, arteries carrying blood outward, veins returning it, and the two sides of the heart circulating distinct streams between the body and the lungs. He had been working on the theory for nearly two decades and had presented earlier versions in lectures. The medical establishment largely ignored the book for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: 1628 — William Harvey, "Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus." Harvey's practice lost patients initially as word spread of his heresy. He lived long enough to see the theory accepted; he died in 1657 at 79, still personally treating King Charles II.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: Human Genome Draft Published
events.blurb: Two groups — the international Human Genome Project consortium and the private company Celera Genomics, which had entered the race late with a competing methodology — simultaneously published their draft sequences of the 3 billion base pairs of the human genome in the journals Nature and Science. The entries were the culmination of 11 years of work and a vast investment of computing and laboratory resources. Humans had roughly 21,000 genes — far fewer than most biologists had predicted.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 2001 — publications in Nature (consortium) and Science (Celera). The "finished" version of the sequence arrived in 2003. Sequencing a human genome now costs about $200 (down from $2.7 billion) and takes a day.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest Completed
events.blurb: A Greco-Roman astronomer working in Alexandria compiled the most comprehensive mathematical model of the heavens yet assembled, describing the apparent motions of the Sun, Moon, planets, and 1,022 fixed stars using a system of circles and epicycles centred on the Earth. The work synthesised centuries of Babylonian and Greek observations and provided a predictive model accurate enough to calculate planetary positions centuries into the future.
events.revealBlurb: c. 150 CE — the Almagest was so complete that it suppressed further progress in astronomy for over a millennium. Astronomers kept patching it rather than questioning its Earth-centred premise. The name comes from the Arabic al-majisṭī, meaning "the greatest" — added by Islamic scholars who translated and preserved the text when European copies were lost.

events.title: Radioactivity Discovered
events.blurb: A French physicist studying uranium salts placed a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer alongside a uranium sample during several cloudy days, expecting to run a sunlight experiment later. When he developed the plate anyway, he found a sharp image — proving the uranium was spontaneously emitting invisible radiation with no external energy source, a phenomenon no existing theory could explain.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1896 — Henri Becquerel announced to the Academy of Sciences that the image was "very distinct." The discovery was accidental: bad weather cancelled his planned sunlight experiment. He initially thought it was a variant of X-rays; it took the Curies to show radioactivity was a property of the atom itself.

events.title: Cosmic Microwave Background Detected
events.blurb: Two radio astronomers testing a sensitive antenna at a New Jersey laboratory detected an inexplicable low-level microwave hiss coming equally from every direction in the sky, regardless of season or time of day. Unable to explain it as noise — including suspected pigeon droppings on the antenna — they eventually learned that theorists nearby had predicted exactly such radiation as the afterglow of the universe's earliest moments.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1964 — Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson initially assumed the noise was instrument error or interference from New York City. They famously removed a pair of pigeons that had nested in the antenna and cleaned out the "white dielectric material." The theorists at Princeton, who had been preparing to search for the signal, were beaten to the discovery.

events.title: Higgs Boson Announced
events.blurb: At a packed seminar, two independent experimental teams working at the world's largest particle accelerator announced the observation of a new particle consistent with the long-predicted Higgs boson — the quantum field excitation that gives other fundamental particles their mass. The discovery completed the standard model of particle physics, confirming a prediction made nearly fifty years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 2012 — Peter Higgs, who had predicted the boson in 1964, was in the audience and reportedly wept. The two experiments — ATLAS and CMS — had been run in blind competition to avoid bias. Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: Rhapsody in Blue Premieres
events.blurb: A 25-year-old former Tin Pan Alley song-plugger's first major concert work — a one-movement concerto for piano and jazz band — premiered at a Manhattan concert hall advertised as "An Experiment in Modern Music." The piece's opening clarinet glissando, improvised in rehearsal as a joke, was left in. The concert had begun with banal novelty pieces; by the time the composer walked out to sit at the piano, the audience was dozing. He woke them up.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1924 — George Gershwin at Aeolian Hall, Manhattan. The bandleader was Paul Whiteman. The audience included Rachmaninoff, Stravinsky, Fritz Kreisler, and Sergei Rachmaninoff. United Airlines has used it as its ad music since 1987.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Hip-Hop Born in the Bronx
events.blurb: An 18-year-old Jamaican-born DJ, using two turntables to extend the instrumental breaks of funk and soul records, played his younger sister's back-to-school party in the rec room of a public housing building in the South Bronx. His technique of looping drum breaks became the foundation of hip-hop. The party went so well that he began DJ-ing at local parks and block parties; rappers (then called MCs) began performing over his sets. A new culture was born.
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 1973 — DJ Kool Herc (Clive Campbell) at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, the Bronx. The address is now a national historic site. Herc's "merry-go-round" technique of using two copies of the same record to loop the break is still the foundation of every hip-hop DJ set.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: Dot-com Crash
events.blurb: The NASDAQ Composite index, which had quintupled in five years on the back of unprofitable but enthusiastic internet stocks, peaked at 5,048 on a Friday morning and began a two-and-a-half-year decline that would erase nearly 78 percent of its value. Companies founded on the premise of "eyeballs" rather than revenue disappeared within months; venture capital dried up; several hundred thousand tech workers lost their jobs.
events.revealBlurb: March 10, 2000 — the NASDAQ peak. It would not regain that level until April 2015. Pets.com became the poster child of dot-com excess, burning through $300 million in 18 months to sell pet food online at a loss.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: McCarthy Wheeling Speech
events.blurb: At a Lincoln Day dinner in West Virginia, a previously obscure U.S. senator brandished a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known communists working in the State Department. The charge, later revised repeatedly and never substantiated, launched a four-year domestic witch-hunt that would bear his name.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1950 — Joseph McCarthy, up for re-election, stumbled onto his signature issue. The "list" he waved kept changing: 205, then 57, then 81. No copy of the original was ever produced. It destroyed thousands of careers anyway.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Warsaw Pact Founded
events.blurb: Eight communist-bloc nations signed a mutual defense treaty in the Polish capital, creating a military alliance explicitly framed as a response to West Germany's admission into the rival Atlantic alliance ten days earlier. In practice, it institutionalized Soviet command over the armed forces of its eastern European satellites.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1955 — members included the USSR, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and Albania. It was dissolved in July 1991, six months before the USSR itself vanished. Most of its former members are now in NATO.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Soviet Invasion of Afghanistan
events.blurb: Thousands of Soviet paratroopers and mechanized divisions crossed into a central Asian country to prop up a failing Marxist government, assassinating the sitting president in the process and installing a more pliable replacement. The operation was supposed to last weeks. Instead it dragged on for nearly a decade, bleeding the Soviet treasury, radicalizing a generation of fighters, and helping bring the superpower down.
events.revealBlurb: December 24-27, 1979 — the intervention cost the USSR an estimated 15,000 dead and 35,000 wounded. The US, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan funneled billions in arms to the mujahideen, some of whom would later form al-Qaeda.

events.title: Ashoka Conquers Kalinga
events.blurb: A Mauryan emperor's army conquered a fiercely resistant coastal kingdom after a war that, by the emperor's own inscriptions, killed 100,000 people and displaced 150,000 more. Revolted by the carnage he had ordered, the emperor publicly renounced war, embraced a philosophy of non-violence, and had pillars erected across his realm inscribed with edicts of compassion — the earliest dateable Indian texts we can read today.
events.revealBlurb: c. 261 BCE — Ashoka the Great, Maurya dynasty. The lion capital from his pillar at Sarnath — four lions standing back to back — is now India's national emblem.

events.title: Aryabhata Writes the Aryabhatiya
events.blurb: A 23-year-old mathematician in Kusumapura (near modern Patna) completed a treatise of 118 verses that calculated pi as 3.1416, explained lunar and solar eclipses geometrically, asserted that the Earth rotates on its axis — not the stars — and introduced the concept of a place-value system that would eventually become the decimal notation used worldwide today. He also calculated the length of the sidereal year accurate to within a few minutes.
events.revealBlurb: 499 CE — Aryabhata, Gupta period, Pataliputra. ISRO named its first satellite "Aryabhata" in 1975. His value of pi was so accurate that it was not surpassed in Europe for another thousand years. He also correctly said the Earth is round and rotates — in 499 CE.

events.title: Muhammad Ghori Defeats Prithviraj Chauhan
events.blurb: At a plain north of Delhi, the same ground where a year earlier the Rajput king had repelled the same invader, a feigned Afghan retreat drew the Rajput cavalry forward and out of formation. Encircling cavalry cut off the scattered horsemen, and by evening the most powerful Hindu king of north India had been captured and subsequently executed. The result ended 350 years of Rajput dominance and opened the Gangetic plain to Islamic rule.
events.revealBlurb: 1192 CE — Muhammad of Ghor vs. Prithviraj Chauhan III, Battle of Tarain (modern Taraori, Haryana). Prithviraj is remembered in a 12th-century Hindi ballad, the Prithviraj Raso. In folklore, the defeated king shot an arrow through the sound of Ghori's voice alone — blind, in captivity — guided by a bard who called out the target's position.

events.title: Akbar Secures the Mughal Throne
events.blurb: A 13-year-old Mughal prince was crowned emperor at Kalanaur, Punjab, moments after his father fell down a library staircase in Delhi. His regent Bairam Khan immediately faced a formidable rival — the Hindu general Hemu, who had taken Delhi with 30,000 cavalry and 1,500 war elephants. At the second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was felled by a stray arrow mid-battle, his army collapsed, and the boy king's empire was saved.
events.revealBlurb: February 1556 CE — Akbar the Great. The same king who would later abolish the jizya tax, marry Rajput princesses, invent a syncretic religion, and reportedly have three thousand women in his harem started his reign as a frightened teenager hiding behind his general.

events.title: Guru Arjan Dev Is Executed by Mughal Order
events.blurb: The fifth Sikh Guru, who had compiled the Adi Granth and built the Golden Temple, was arrested by the Mughal emperor on charges of blessing a rebel prince. Ordered to pay a fine of 200,000 rupees and alter his scripture's hymns, he refused both. He was then tortured over several days — made to sit on a burning iron plate while red-hot sand was poured over his body — and died in Lahore. His execution permanently changed the relationship between the Sikh Panth and Mughal power.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 1606 CE — Guru Arjan Dev Ji, Lahore, Mughal Empire under Jahangir. His martyrdom led his successor, Guru Hargobind, to take up two swords — one of spiritual authority, one of temporal power — and build an armed Sikh army.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Mongol Sack of Baghdad
events.blurb: A Mongol army under a grandson of Genghis Khan besieged a Mesopotamian capital that had been the cultural and financial center of the Islamic world for five centuries. The city fell after thirteen days. The caliph was wrapped in a carpet and trampled by horses; the House of Wisdom was burned. Witnesses said the Tigris ran black for days with the ink of destroyed books, then red with the blood of their authors.
events.revealBlurb: February 10, 1258 — Hulagu Khan. Estimates of the dead range from 90,000 to over a million. The Abbasid Caliphate as a political power died with the city; Islamic civilization's center of gravity shifted permanently to Cairo and later Constantinople.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Britney Shaves Her Head
events.blurb: A 25-year-old American pop star walked into a Los Angeles hair salon at 8 PM, asked a stylist to shave her head completely, and when the stylist refused, picked up the electric clippers and did it herself. Paparazzi captured the scene through the salon window. Images went global within hours, becoming an emblem of a period of intensely public personal struggle — divorce, custody battles, reportage, and tabloid harassment. She would be placed under conservatorship nine months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 2007 — Britney Spears at Esther's Haircutting Studio, Tarzana, CA. The conservatorship lasted 13 years, ending in November 2021 after the #FreeBritney movement. Her 2023 memoir "The Woman in Me" describes the head-shaving as a reaction to feeling over-managed and pressured by the industry.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Whitney Houston Dies
events.blurb: A 48-year-old American singer with one of the most powerful voices in pop music history was found unresponsive in a bathtub at a Beverly Hills hotel. The cause of death was accidental drowning complicated by heart disease and cocaine use. She had been scheduled to attend a Grammy Awards pre-party that evening. Her death came the night before the Grammys themselves, which had to be hastily rewritten to include a tribute. Seven years later her only daughter would die under similar circumstances.
events.revealBlurb: February 11, 2012 — Whitney Houston at the Beverly Hilton. Daughter Bobbi Kristina Brown, 22, was found unresponsive in a bathtub on January 31, 2015 and died six months later. Houston's "I Will Always Love You" had been the bestselling single by a woman in history until Adele surpassed it.

events.title: David Bowie Dies
events.blurb: A 69-year-old English singer and songwriter died of liver cancer at his New York apartment, two days after releasing what turned out to be his final studio album. The album's cover art, title ("Blackstar"), and lyrics — which in retrospect clearly addressed death — had been a farewell that almost nobody had caught in real time. His decades of genre-shifting personas, starting with the glam-rock Ziggy Stardust in 1972, had made him one of the most influential musicians of the late 20th century. His death prompted an international wave of mourning.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 2016 — David Bowie (David Robert Jones). Diagnosed 18 months earlier; kept the illness private. His final public appearance was at the premiere of his off-Broadway musical "Lazarus" in December 2015. 2016 became known as a year of many significant music deaths.

events.title: Harambe Killed
events.blurb: A 17-year-old western lowland gorilla at the Cincinnati Zoo was shot and killed by zoo staff after a 3-year-old boy climbed through a barrier and fell into the gorilla enclosure. The zoo explained that the gorilla had grabbed the child and dragged him through the water; tranquilizer darts would have taken too long. The killing triggered a wave of online outrage, internet memes, and several years' worth of "RIP Harambe" jokes that became a meta-joke of 2010s internet culture.
events.revealBlurb: May 28, 2016 — Harambe, Cincinnati Zoo. The child recovered fully. The zoo director Thane Maynard defended the decision as the only available option. The Harambe meme's peculiar staying power has been studied as a case of absurdist internet grief; election-poll write-in votes for Harambe persisted for years.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: Fall of Singapore
events.blurb: An island fortress considered impregnable from the sea fell in one week when attackers crossed a narrow strait at its land-facing back and advanced down a peninsula faster than anyone had thought possible. The surrender of 80,000 troops in a single capitulation stands as the largest in the history of the British Army.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1942. General Percival surrendered at 6:20 PM. Churchill called it "the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history." The great naval guns of Singapore pointed seaward and many lacked armour-piercing shells anyway — the attack had come from the wrong direction entirely.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: First Nuclear Chain Reaction
events.blurb: In a squash court beneath a university stadium, a team of physicists assembled 45,000 carefully machined blocks of graphite around pellets of uranium into a lattice the size of a house, withdrew a control rod, and achieved humanity's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — completing the key step toward a new category of weapon.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1942, under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. Enrico Fermi's team celebrated with a bottle of Chianti in paper cups. The coded telegram sent to Washington read: "The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World." The reactor sat in a populated neighbourhood with no containment vessel.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: Pyaasa Released
events.blurb: A poet who the city believes to be dead wanders through venal publishers and indifferent relatives in a film Guru Dutt both directed and starred in, constructing one of Indian cinema's most sustained indictments of commercialised culture through Sahir Ludhianvi's Urdu verse set to S.D. Burman's music. Time magazine later placed it among the 100 greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1957 — Guru Dutt's masterwork. The film was semi-autobiographical; Dutt was increasingly alienated from the Bombay film industry's values, an estrangement he did not survive — he died in 1964, aged 39. The song "Jaane Woh Kaise Log The" remains among the most covered in Hindi film music.

events.title: 3 Idiots Released
events.blurb: A comedy about three engineering students raging against rote-learning and parental ambition broke every domestic box-office record on its first day, earned over ₹460 crore worldwide, and set the US box-office record for an Indian film with $4.8 million from 120 American theatres. Its two-word catchphrase — "Aal izz well" — entered everyday Indian speech almost immediately.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 2009 — directed by Rajkumar Hirani, loosely based on Chetan Bhagat's novel Five Point Someone. Aamir Khan, then 44, played a college student. The film triggered a genuine policy conversation about India's education system and student mental health.

events.title: Slumdog Millionaire Wins Best Picture
events.blurb: A British-directed film set entirely in Mumbai — shot partly in the Dharavi slum with non-professional child actors, partly in the chaos of the city's streets — swept eight Oscars including Best Picture at the 81st Academy Awards, making it the first film primarily set and cast in India to win the top prize. Its pavement-to-riches structure was lifted directly from Bollywood's own playbook.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 2009. Directed by Danny Boyle. A.R. Rahman won Best Original Score and Best Original Song for "Jai Ho" — his first Oscars, received in the same night. The child actors from the film were discovered to be living in poverty after production wrapped, triggering international headlines.

events.title: Jawan Released
events.blurb: A Tamil director's Hindi-film debut — a dual-role action thriller mixing vigilante politics with hospital corruption — earned ₹75 crore on its opening day, making it the highest-opening-day gross in Hindi cinema at the time, then crossed ₹600 crore domestically, becoming the first Hindi film to do so. Its release capped a year in which its star reclaimed the top of the industry after a decade's absence.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 2023 — directed by Atlee. Shah Rukh Khan's return, following Pathaan earlier that year, made 2023 the most commercially dominant single-year performance by any one actor in Bollywood history. The film's opening credits featured cameos by over thirty prominent South Indian actors.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Completed
events.blurb: A German goldsmith completed printing a 1,286-page Latin Bible using a press with movable metal type, producing an estimated 180 copies at a rate no scribe could approach. Each sheet required individually set letter blocks cast in an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — making it the first book in Europe produced by mechanical movable type.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: ENIAC Unveiled
events.blurb: Engineers at an American university publicly demonstrated an 27-tonne general-purpose electronic computer, filling a 30 by 15 metre room with 17,468 vacuum tubes, 10,000 capacitors, and 6,000 switches. The machine calculated artillery-shell trajectories 2,400 times faster than a human with an adding machine. Programming it required physically rewiring hundreds of cables; the programmers — all women — had to crawl inside to swap plugs.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1946 — University of Pennsylvania. Designers J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly. Programmers: Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas, and Ruth Lichterman. They were not invited to the unveiling dinner; their faces were cropped out of celebratory photos for decades.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Watson Wins Jeopardy
events.blurb: An IBM supercomputer named after the company's founder competed over three nights of a televised American trivia game show against the two greatest human champions the show had ever produced — and won by a wide margin. The machine had been fed a corpus of Wikipedia, encyclopedias, and dictionaries; it processed buzzer-triggered natural-language clues with a complex pipeline of heuristics and statistical models. It was not a single breakthrough; it was an engineering triumph.
events.revealBlurb: February 14-16, 2011 — Watson vs. Ken Jennings and Brad Rutter. Jennings' final written answer on night three: "I, for one, welcome our new computer overlords." IBM spent heavily trying to commercialize Watson for healthcare and business; most of those products have since been divested or discontinued.

events.title: Elizabeth Blackwell Graduates
events.blurb: A 28-year-old English-born schoolteacher, who had been admitted to a small upstate New York medical college as a joke when the all-male student body voted unanimously to accept her application, graduated first in her class to become the first woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. She had been refused admission by 20 other schools. Her younger sister would become the third.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1849 — Geneva Medical College, Geneva, NY. No American hospital would employ her; she moved to Paris and London for clinical training. She later founded a medical college for women and practiced for decades, treating patients the profession otherwise ignored.

events.title: New Zealand Grants Women's Suffrage
events.blurb: The governor of a British colony in the South Pacific gave royal assent to an electoral act adding "and women" to the existing definition of qualified voters, making the colony the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the national franchise. Roughly 90,000 women registered within weeks; 82 percent of them turned out for the first subsequent election.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1893 — campaigners including Kate Sheppard delivered a petition a quarter of a kilometre long with nearly 32,000 signatures. The date is now Suffrage Day in New Zealand. Sheppard appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

events.title: The Feminine Mystique Published
events.blurb: A former labour journalist who had been writing articles for women's magazines published a 410-page book analyzing what she called "the problem that has no name" — the stifling dissatisfaction of educated suburban housewives. It sold three million copies within three years and became the foundational text of a resurgent American feminist movement that would transform employment law, education policy, and reproductive rights.
events.revealBlurb: February 19, 1963 — Betty Friedan. The book drew on her research into a Smith College alumni survey. Friedan went on to co-found the National Organization for Women in 1966 and help lead the 1970 Women's Strike for Equality.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: #MeToo Goes Viral
events.blurb: Five days after a major U.S. newspaper published a long investigation into sexual harassment and assault allegations against a powerful Hollywood film producer, an actress posted on Twitter asking women who had been sexually harassed or assaulted to reply with two words. Within 24 hours, those two words had been used 500,000 times on Twitter alone. The phrase had been coined a decade earlier by a Black activist working with survivors in the American South.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2017 — Alyssa Milano's tweet; the phrase was coined in 2006 by Tarana Burke. The producer was Harvey Weinstein, finally convicted of rape in February 2020. A cascade of resignations, prosecutions, and cultural reckoning followed across industries.

events.title: Bannister's 4-Minute Mile
events.blurb: A 25-year-old medical student in his final year of training, racing on a windy Oxford track in a university-versus-amateur competition, ran a mile in 3 minutes and 59.4 seconds — the first human ever to break the four-minute barrier. The record stood for 46 days. His pacers, who trailed off at the halfway and three-quarter marks on a pre-arranged plan, were athletes the newspapers had not noticed. Sport doctors had warned a sub-four mile might be physiologically impossible.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1954 — Roger Bannister at Iffley Road track. Pacers: Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. John Landy of Australia broke Bannister's record 46 days later. Bannister beat him in the "Mile of the Century" race at the Vancouver Commonwealth Games in August 1954 — both running sub-four.

events.title: Cassius Clay Shocks Liston
events.blurb: A 22-year-old loud-talking boxer from Louisville, a 7-1 underdog against the seemingly invincible heavyweight champion, danced around his opponent for six rounds, cut him under the eye in the third, and won the world title when the champion refused to answer the bell for the seventh round. He skipped around the ring shouting "I am the greatest!" to reporters who had mostly written him off as doomed. He would change his name to one the world would remember the next morning.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1964 — Cassius Clay defeated Sonny Liston in Miami Beach. Clay announced his new name, Muhammad Ali, two days later, having joined the Nation of Islam. He would win 56 of his 61 professional bouts and lose his prime years to a Vietnam War draft controversy.

events.title: The Rumble in the Jungle
events.blurb: A 32-year-old heavyweight boxing challenger, widely predicted to lose to the younger and vastly more powerful champion, leaned back against the ropes for seven rounds and absorbed punishing body blows — a tactic he later nicknamed "rope-a-dope." In the 8th, when the champion visibly tired, the challenger delivered a flurry of punches that knocked him out. The fight was held in an African capital as part of a pioneering pan-African promotion.
events.revealBlurb: October 30, 1974 — Muhammad Ali KO'd George Foreman at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo). Promoter Don King organized it. The event was immortalized in the 1996 documentary "When We Were Kings."

events.title: Miracle on Ice
events.blurb: A U.S. college-aged men's hockey team, facing a Soviet Union team that had won five of the previous six Olympic gold medals and was widely considered the best in the world, won 4-3 at a Lake Placid Winter Olympics with a third-period game-winning goal by the team's captain. The victory, during a tense period of Cold War tensions and a national recession, was broadcast on delayed tape; the announcer's closing cry — "Do you believe in miracles? YES!" — became one of the most-replayed lines in American sports.
events.revealBlurb: February 22, 1980 — US vs USSR at the Lake Placid Olympics. Coach: Herb Brooks. The US went on to win the gold medal by beating Finland two days later. The captain was Mike Eruzione. Al Michaels was the ABC announcer.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Army-McCarthy Hearings
events.blurb: A televised congressional inquiry pit a grandstanding senator against the U.S. Army, which he had accused of harboring subversives. Over 36 days, 20 million Americans watched live as his bullying tactics eroded public sympathy. The defining moment came when a quiet Boston lawyer turned to him and asked, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
events.revealBlurb: April 22 to June 17, 1954 — the lawyer was Joseph Welch. His line came on June 9, after McCarthy attacked a young associate. Six months later the Senate voted 67-22 to censure McCarthy. He drank himself to death within three years.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: Nixon Visits China
events.blurb: A U.S. president whose entire career had been built on anti-communist credentials stepped off Air Force One in the Chinese capital to shake hands with the leader of a nation Washington had refused to recognize for 23 years. The week-long visit, carefully choreographed after two years of secret diplomacy, upended the bipolar world order and drove a wedge between the two great communist powers.
events.revealBlurb: February 21-28, 1972 — Richard Nixon meets Mao Zedong. Henry Kissinger had flown secretly to Beijing via Pakistan the previous summer to arrange it. The phrase "Nixon goes to China" has since become shorthand for a politician doing something only his base could forgive.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: Berlin Wall Falls
events.blurb: An East German government spokesman announced at a press conference that citizens could cross the border immediately, triggering jubilant crowds who arrived at checkpoints and began dismantling the 155-kilometre concrete barrier with hammers and their bare hands. More than two million East Germans crossed into West Berlin during the following weekend alone.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street."
