Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: James Meredith at Ole Miss
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Air Force veteran, after a year of legal battles, became the first Black student to enroll at a Mississippi university with a deep segregationist tradition. His arrival on campus sparked a night-long riot by a mob of 3,000 whites that killed two people and injured hundreds. Federal marshals and troops protected him through graduation.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1962 — Oxford, Mississippi. President Kennedy sent 30,000 federal troops, the largest domestic military deployment since the Civil War. Governor Ross Barnett had personally tried to block Meredith four times. Meredith graduated with a degree in political science.

events.title: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing
events.blurb: A dynamite bomb planted by Klansmen exploded under the stone steps of a Black church in a Southern city on a Sunday morning, minutes before the 11:00 service. Four girls preparing for choir in the basement were killed; 22 others were injured. The bombing, eighteen days after the March on Washington, hardened national public opinion and accelerated passage of civil rights legislation.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. Victims: Addie Mae Collins, 14; Carol Denise McNair, 11; Carole Robertson, 14; Cynthia Wesley, 14. The four Klansmen responsible were slowly prosecuted over four decades; the last conviction came in 2002.

events.title: Malcolm X Assassinated
events.blurb: A charismatic Black Muslim minister who had broken with the Nation of Islam a year earlier was shot 21 times by three gunmen as he rose to address an audience at a Harlem ballroom. He was 39. The three men convicted of the killing included two who were demonstrably not at the scene; their convictions were overturned in 2021 after a decades-long campaign by their families and a Netflix documentary.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1965 — Audubon Ballroom, Manhattan. Malcolm had suffered an assassination attempt at his home a week earlier. His autobiography, co-written with Alex Haley and published posthumously, remains required reading in American universities.

events.title: George Floyd Murdered
events.blurb: A 46-year-old Black man was killed in a Midwestern American city when a white police officer kneeled on his neck for 9 minutes and 29 seconds while he was handcuffed face-down on the pavement. A 17-year-old bystander filmed the entire encounter on her phone. The video triggered the largest protest movement in American history — 15 to 26 million people marched across all 50 states over the following weeks.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 2020 — Minneapolis, officer Derek Chauvin. The bystander was Darnella Frazier; she received a Pulitzer Prize special citation. Chauvin was convicted of second-degree murder 11 months later and sentenced to 22 years. Protests spread to more than 60 countries.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Enigma Broken at Bletchley
events.blurb: A team of mathematicians and linguists working in a cluttered hut in the English countryside deployed an electromechanical machine that could test thousands of rotor settings per minute, cracking the daily-changed cipher used by an opposing military's command and logistics networks — and began reading intercepted messages within hours of their transmission.
events.revealBlurb: May 1940 — Bletchley Park's upgraded Bombe, designed by Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman, began breaking Luftwaffe "Red" traffic daily. The secret was so tightly held that some commanders were fed cover stories about lucky reconnaissance flights. The intelligence was codenamed Ultra and arguably shortened the conflict by two years.

events.title: Operation Barbarossa
events.blurb: Three million soldiers, 600,000 motorised vehicles, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft crossed a 2,900-kilometre border in the pre-dawn darkness, launching the largest land invasion in military history. The defender's air force lost over a thousand planes in the first day, many of them still on the ground.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1941. Stalin reportedly refused to believe his own border commanders' early reports and assumed the attacks were unauthorised provocations. The operation's codename referenced the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. By December, Germany had advanced 1,000 km but failed to knock the Soviet Union out of the war.

events.title: Flag Raising on Iwo Jima
events.blurb: A photograph taken on a volcanic island's highest point captured six men raising a large flag over rubble and smoke, becoming one of the most reproduced images in history — and the model for a national memorial — though the battle it symbolised had barely begun and would last another five weeks at a cost exceeding 26,000 American casualties.
events.revealBlurb: February 23, 1945 — Joe Rosenthal's photograph was actually of the second flag raised that day; a smaller flag had gone up hours earlier. Three of the six men in the photograph were killed before the island was secured. Admiral Chester Nimitz observed: "Among the Americans who served on Iwo Jima, uncommon valor was a common virtue."

events.title: Execution of Mussolini
events.blurb: The founder of one of the 20th century's major fascist movements was captured hiding in a German military convoy while attempting to flee across a northern border, taken to a lakeside village by communist partisans, and shot 26 hours later — his body then transported to a major city and hung upside down at a petrol station for public display.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 1945 — executed at Giulino di Mezzegra on Lake Como, two days before Hitler's death. Mussolini and his mistress Clara Petacci were shot, then driven to Milan and strung up by their heels at the Piazzale Loreto — the same square where partisan hostages had been publicly displayed by Fascists a year earlier.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Caning of Senator Charles Sumner
events.blurb: Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina strode onto the Senate floor and beat Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts unconscious with a metal-topped gutta-percha cane, inflicting such severe head injuries that Sumner could not return to his seat for over three years. The assault came two days after Sumner delivered a blistering antislavery speech mocking Brooks's cousin; Massachusetts left Sumner's empty desk on display as a rebuke.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1856 — U.S. Senate chamber. Brooks resigned, was immediately re-elected by South Carolina, and received commemorative canes inscribed "Hit Him Again." Sumner's empty desk served as visible propaganda for the antislavery cause for three years. The incident convinced many Northerners that slavery corrupted men beyond reason.

events.title: Emancipation Proclamation Takes Effect
events.blurb: President Abraham Lincoln's executive order declaring freedom for all enslaved people in Confederate states in active rebellion took legal effect at the new year, transforming the character of the war from a constitutional dispute over secession into an explicit struggle over slavery. The proclamation did not free enslaved people in border states still in the Union, but it authorized the enlistment of Black men into the Union Army — eventually nearly 200,000 would serve.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 1863 — Washington, D.C. Lincoln spent the morning shaking hundreds of hands at a White House reception; by the time he sat down to sign the Proclamation his hand trembled so badly he paused. "If my name ever goes into history it will be for this act," he said.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education Ruling
events.blurb: A unanimous Supreme Court held that racially segregated public schools were inherently unequal and violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson doctrine of "separate but equal." The unanimous 9–0 decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren after months of behind-the-scenes persuasion, applied to all public schools and laid the legal foundation for desegregation across American society.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Washington, D.C. Chief Justice Warren had been appointed by Eisenhower, who privately thought the ruling a mistake. The lead attorney for the plaintiffs was Thurgood Marshall — who would later become the first Black justice on the very court he argued before.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.blurb: Hannibal's army of roughly 50,000 men destroyed a Roman force of 80,000 in a single afternoon by letting the Roman center push forward into a concave line, then closing cavalry on both flanks until the entire legionary mass was encircled and butchered. Between 55,000 and 70,000 Romans died; senators threw handfuls of gold rings stripped from dead equestrians into a bowl to show Carthage the scale of the slaughter.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 216 BCE, Apulia. The double-envelopment Hannibal used at Cannae became the template studied at military academies for 2,000 years. Hannibal's war elephants, his most famous asset, had all died before this battle.

events.title: Han Dynasty Founded
events.blurb: A former peasant who had risen through the collapsing Qin military to become a rebel general defeated his principal rival in a civil war and declared himself emperor, founding a dynasty that would rule China for four centuries. The Han synthesized Confucian political theory with Qin administrative machinery, ran the Silk Road trade with the West, invented paper, cast iron plowshares, and effectively defined the imperial Chinese civilization that would persist until 1911. The ethnic majority of modern China still calls itself "Han."
events.revealBlurb: 202 BCE — Liu Bang, posthumously Emperor Gaozu. He defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia. The Han dynasty is conventionally divided into the Western Han (202 BCE - 9 CE) and Eastern Han (25 CE - 220 CE), with a brief Wang Mang interregnum between.

events.title: Madonna's "Like a Prayer" Video
events.blurb: The music video for a 30-year-old singer's new single, featuring burning crosses, stigmata, and the singer kissing a Black saint statue coming to life, premiered during a Pepsi commercial at the start of a television special paid for by the soft-drink company. The Vatican condemned the video as blasphemous; conservative Christian groups organized boycotts; Pepsi paid the singer $5 million to sever their sponsorship deal. Her album sold 15 million copies.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1989 — the Pepsi commercial; the full video premiered on MTV March 3. Director Mary Lambert. The controversy gave Madonna an estimated $5 million for the Pepsi deal plus enormous free publicity; she kept the money. The album "Like a Prayer" remains her best-reviewed.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Bronco Chase
events.blurb: A 46-year-old former football star, charged with the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, failed to surrender to police at the agreed time. A friend drove him along a Los Angeles freeway in a white Ford Bronco at around 55 km/h, pursued by police cruisers and a dozen news helicopters. An estimated 95 million Americans watched the chase live on television. It ended with his surrender at his home.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1994 — O.J. Simpson, driver Al Cowlings. NBC interrupted Game 5 of the NBA Finals between the Knicks and Rockets to show the chase. Simpson was acquitted of murder on October 3, 1995 in what was nicknamed the "Trial of the Century."

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Seinfeld Finale
events.blurb: The 180th and final episode of a nine-year NBC sitcom about petty New York narcissists aired to 76 million viewers. The divisive finale had the four main characters put on trial in a fictional Massachusetts town for failing to help a carjacking victim, watched by a parade of minor characters from earlier seasons who had been wronged by them. Critics and fans were largely disappointed; its creator defended it as consistent with the show's amoral premise.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1998 — "The Finale." Written by Larry David, returning after leaving the show in 1996. Ad slots on the finale sold for around $2 million for 30 seconds — a pre-Super Bowl record for a TV program.

events.title: Furby Released
events.blurb: A battery-operated toy furry pet that could speak, move its eyes, and apparently learn English words from "Furbish" over time became the must-have Christmas gift of the season. Parents who had lived through the Cabbage Patch Kids and Tickle Me Elmo crazes of previous years went through it again. The National Security Agency banned them from their premises, reportedly out of concern that they might record classified conversations and "repeat" them.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1998 — Tiger Electronics. 40 million Furbys sold in the first three years. The NSA's ban was based on a misunderstanding of the toy's technology — it had no recording capability at all; "learning" was a pre-programmed script that made the toy seem to become more English-speaking over time.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: The Tale of Genji
events.blurb: A Japanese noblewoman serving at the imperial court of a Heian-era empress completed a 54-chapter prose narrative following the life, loves, and political career of a fictional son of an emperor. Full of psychological interiority, metaphorical poetry, and a sophisticated unreliable narrator, it is widely regarded as the world's first modern novel. It was written over more than a decade and circulated in manuscript among the court.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1010 CE — Murasaki Shikibu. The earliest surviving complete manuscript dates from the 13th century. It has been translated into English several times; Arthur Waley's 1925-33 version introduced it to the West, but recent translations are preferred for accuracy.

events.title: The Communist Manifesto
events.blurb: A 29-year-old German-born philosopher-journalist and his 27-year-old industrialist-heir collaborator published a 23-page political pamphlet commissioned by a small London-based workers' organization. Its opening sentence — about a spectre haunting Europe — and its closing rallying cry became arguably the most politically consequential prose of the 19th century. Within three weeks, revolutions were breaking out across the continent.
events.revealBlurb: February 21, 1848 — Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. The League of the Just commissioned it. The 1848 revolutions failed; the Manifesto didn't become widely read until the 1872 edition with a new preface. By the 20th century it had shaped the political systems of a third of humanity.

events.title: Walden Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Massachusetts essayist, graduate of Harvard, former schoolteacher, and occasional pencil-factory worker, published an account of two years and two months he had spent living in a cabin he had built himself beside a glacier-pond near Concord. The book mixed natural observation, economic criticism, and philosophical reflection. It sold slowly; its reputation grew after the author's early death seven years later, and he is now considered one of the founders of American nature writing.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1854 — Henry David Thoreau. He had lived at Walden Pond 1845-47. The pond was, contrary to legend, a short walk from his family home; his mother did his laundry. Thoreau's civil-disobedience essay would later inspire Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Eyjafjallajökull Eruption
events.blurb: A glacier-capped volcano in Iceland erupted, sending a plume of fine silicate ash into the jet stream. Authorities across Europe, uncertain about engine safety, grounded all commercial aviation for six days. Around 10 million passengers were stranded, and global airlines lost an estimated $1.7 billion. Few people died, but the event showed how fragile modern mobility had become.
events.revealBlurb: April 14-20, 2010 — Iceland. The volcano's name became a running joke for newscasters. Stranded travelers included heads of state on their way to a funeral in Poland; many drove for days to get home. Rental car companies had their biggest week ever.

events.title: Typhoon Haiyan
events.blurb: One of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall — with sustained winds of 315 km/h — struck the central Philippines, obliterating coastal cities. A 7-metre storm surge drove ships onto city streets; the city of Tacloban lost most of its infrastructure. At least 6,300 people died, and 4 million were displaced.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2013 — Leyte province. The Filipino lead negotiator at the UN climate talks that week gave a tearful speech and began a hunger strike until "meaningful progress" was made. His country's delegation wore black.

events.title: Beirut Port Explosion
events.blurb: 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate that had been haphazardly stored in a warehouse at a Mediterranean capital's port for six years detonated after a smaller fire reached it. The blast was felt 240 kilometres away in Cyprus, killed 218 people, injured 7,000, and left 300,000 homeless. It ranks among the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded.
events.revealBlurb: August 4, 2020 — Beirut, Lebanon. The chemicals had been offloaded from a Russian ship in 2013 and simply abandoned. The blast crater was 124 metres wide. Years later no senior official has faced trial; the investigation has been repeatedly obstructed by politicians named as suspects.

events.title: Faraday Demonstrates Induction
events.blurb: A 40-year-old self-taught English scientist, working in a London institution's basement, wrapped an iron ring with two coils of insulated wire, connected one coil to a battery and the other to a galvanometer, and observed that momentarily closing or opening the battery circuit caused a pulse of current in the other coil. The discovery — electromagnetic induction — was the foundation principle of every electrical generator and transformer ever built.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1831 — Michael Faraday at the Royal Institution. He had been a bookbinder's apprentice with barely any formal schooling; Humphry Davy hired him as a lab assistant and he eclipsed his mentor. He was offered a knighthood twice and the presidency of the Royal Society; he refused both.

events.title: US Transcontinental Railroad Completed
events.blurb: Officials drove a ceremonial golden spike into a rail tie at a desolate spot in Utah, joining rails built eastward from Sacramento by Chinese labourers and rails built westward from the Missouri River by Irish labourers. Travel from New York to San Francisco, previously a six-month journey by wagon or ship, now took a week. The two companies, a state-subsidized joint venture, had raced each other for six years; the route had been set by the Lincoln administration in 1862.
events.revealBlurb: May 10, 1869 — Promontory Summit, Utah. The joining rails were two: Central Pacific from the west, Union Pacific from the east. The spike ceremony was telegraphed to the rest of the country; the "Done" message was the first cross-country news bulletin. The Chinese workers who had done most of the hardest labour were not invited to the ceremony.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: First Moving Assembly Line
events.blurb: A Detroit automobile company introduced a moving chassis-assembly line at its Highland Park plant, cutting the time needed to assemble a car from 12 hours to 93 minutes. The innovation — borrowed in part from Chicago meatpacking "disassembly" lines — let the company slash prices and dramatically increase production. The line's relentless pace was hated by workers; the company had to double wages the following year to keep them on the job.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1913 — Ford Motor Company, Highland Park plant. The $5/day wage (equivalent to about $140/day today) followed on January 5, 1914. Workers' turnover at the plant dropped from 370 percent annually to near zero. The wage offer drew applicants by the thousands; police had to turn away crowds in a near-riot.
